blocks.body:
Water flows from a reservoir $s$ to a city $t$ through a system of one-way pipes, each with a maximum rate. How much water per second can reach the city? An obvious upper bound comes from any set of pipes that, if blocked, would cut the city off: the flow can be no larger than their total capacity. The surprise is that the best such bound is always achieved.

This is the max-flow min-cut theorem. Its proof is also an algorithm, and its integer version turns many problems about matchings and disjoint paths into flow problems. We use directed graphs and graph search from [[graph-algorithms]].

blocks.title: Network and flow
blocks.body:
A network is a directed graph with two special vertices, a source $s$ and a sink $t$, and a capacity $c(u,v) \ge 0$ on each edge $(u,v)$. A flow is an assignment of numbers $f(u,v)$ to the edges such that

1. (capacity) $0 \le f(u,v) \le c(u,v)$ for every edge;
2. (conservation) at every vertex $v \ne s, t$, the total flow in equals the total flow out.

The value $|f|$ is the net flow out of $s$: the flow on edges leaving $s$ minus the flow on edges entering $s$.

blocks.title: Cut
blocks.body:
An $s$–$t$ cut is a partition of the vertices into sets $S$ and $T$ with $s \in S$ and $t \in T$. Its capacity $c(S,T)$ is the sum of the capacities of edges going from $S$ to $T$. Edges from $T$ back to $S$ do not count.

For a flow $f$ write $f(S \to T)$ for the total flow on edges from $S$ to $T$, and $f(T \to S)$ for the reverse direction.

blocks.title: Flow across a cut
blocks.body:
For every flow $f$ and every $s$–$t$ cut $(S,T)$,
$$|f| = f(S \to T) - f(T \to S) \le c(S,T).$$

Add up, over all vertices $v \in S$, the quantity (flow out of $v$) minus (flow into $v$). For $v = s$ this is $|f|$, and for every other $v \in S$ it is 0 by conservation, so the sum is $|f|$. On the other hand, an edge with both ends in $S$ contributes $+f$ at its tail and $-f$ at its head, so cancels. An edge from $S$ to $T$ contributes $+f$ once, and an edge from $T$ to $S$ contributes $-f$ once. Hence the sum equals $f(S \to T) - f(T \to S)$. Finally $f(S \to T) \le c(S,T)$ by the capacity condition and $f(T \to S) \ge 0$.

blocks.title: Why greedy is not enough: residual networks
blocks.body:
A natural idea is to keep finding paths from $s$ to $t$ with spare capacity and pushing flow along them. Consider edges $s \to a$, $s \to b$, $a \to b$, $a \to t$, $b \to t$, all of capacity 1. If we first push 1 unit along $s, a, b, t$, then every $s$–$t$ path in the graph uses a full edge and we are stuck at value 1. But value 2 is possible, along $s, a, t$ and $s, b, t$.

The fix is to allow flow to be sent back, cancelling an earlier choice. Given a flow $f$, the residual network has, for each edge $(u,v)$,

- a forward edge $u \to v$ with residual capacity $c(u,v) - f(u,v)$ if this is positive, and
- a backward edge $v \to u$ with residual capacity $f(u,v)$ if this is positive.

An augmenting path is an $s$–$t$ path in the residual network. Pushing $\delta$ units along it (where $\delta$ is the smallest residual capacity on the path) means increasing $f$ on forward edges and decreasing it on backward edges by $\delta$. Capacities stay respected, conservation still holds at each inner vertex, and the value rises by $\delta$. In the example, after the first path the residual network contains $s \to b \to a \to t$, using the backward edge $b \to a$; pushing 1 unit along it removes the flow on $a \to b$ and gives value 2.

(If the network has both $u \to v$ and $v \to u$, keep their residual edges separate; nothing changes in the argument.)

blocks.title: Max-flow min-cut theorem (Ford–Fulkerson)

blocks.body:
(1 implies 2) An augmenting path would increase the value, so a maximum flow has none.

(2 implies 3) Let $S$ be the set of vertices reachable from $s$ in the residual network and $T$ the rest. Then $t \in T$ since there is no augmenting path. Take an edge $(u,v)$ with $u \in S$, $v \in T$. If $f(u,v) < c(u,v)$ there would be a residual edge $u \to v$ and $v$ would be reachable; so $f(u,v) = c(u,v)$. Take an edge $(v,u)$ with $v \in T$, $u \in S$. If $f(v,u) > 0$ there would be a backward residual edge $u \to v$; so $f(v,u) = 0$. By the previous theorem, $|f| = f(S \to T) - f(T \to S) = c(S,T) - 0$.

(3 implies 1) Every flow $g$ satisfies $|g| \le c(S,T) = |f|$ by the previous theorem.

For a finite network a maximum flow exists: the set of flows is a closed bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^E$ and the value is a continuous function, so it attains its maximum. Applying (1 implies 3) to it gives a cut of the same capacity, and no cut can have smaller capacity than a flow's value.

blocks.title: Integrality theorem
blocks.body: If all capacities are integers, the Ford–Fulkerson method (start from the zero flow and augment while an augmenting path exists) stops after at most $c(\{s\}, V \setminus \{s\})$ augmentations, and the final flow is a maximum flow with every $f(u,v)$ an integer.

By induction all flow values stay integers: residual capacities are then integers, so the bottleneck $\delta$ is a positive integer. Each augmentation therefore raises $|f|$ by at least 1, and $|f|$ can never exceed the capacity of the cut $(\{s\}, V \setminus \{s\})$, so the method stops. When it stops there is no augmenting path, and by the max-flow min-cut theorem the flow is maximum.

blocks.title: Algorithms and modelling tricks
A maximum flow and its certificate
blocks.body: The network has edges $s \to a$ (10), $s \to b$ (8), $a \to b$ (5), $a \to c$ (6), $b \to d$ (9), $c \to t$ (9), $d \to c$ (4), $d \to t$ (7). Find a maximum flow and a cut proving it is maximum.
blocks.solution:
Augment along paths with spare capacity:

1. $s, a, c, t$: bottleneck $a \to c$, push 6.
2. $s, a, b, d, t$: $s \to a$ has 4 left, push 4.
3. $s, b, d, t$: $d \to t$ has 3 left, push 3.
4. $s, b, d, c, t$: $b \to d$ has 2 left, push 2.

Total value $6 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 15$. On the edges: $s \to a$ 10, $s \to b$ 5, $a \to b$ 4, $a \to c$ 6, $b \to d$ 9, $c \to t$ 8, $d \to c$ 2, $d \to t$ 7; at each of $a, b, c, d$ inflow equals outflow.

In the residual network, from $s$ we can reach $b$ (since $s \to b$ has 3 spare) and then $a$ (backward along $a \to b$, which carries 4), but nothing else: $a \to c$ and $b \to d$ are full. So $S = \{s, a, b\}$, and the edges leaving $S$ are $a \to c$ (6) and $b \to d$ (9), total 15. A cut of capacity 15 matches the flow of value 15, so both are optimal.

blocks.title: König's theorem from max-flow min-cut
blocks.body: In a bipartite graph with parts $L$ and $R$, a vertex cover is a set of vertices touching every edge. Prove that the largest matching has the same size as the smallest vertex cover.
blocks.solution:
A matching of size $m$ needs at least $m$ vertices to cover its own edges, which are disjoint, so max matching $\le$ min cover. For the reverse inequality, build a network: edges $s \to u$ of capacity 1 for $u \in L$, edges $v \to t$ of capacity 1 for $v \in R$, and each graph edge $uv$ directed $u \to v$ with a huge capacity, say $|L| + 1$.

By the integrality theorem there is an integer maximum flow; each $u \in L$ receives at most 1 unit, so it uses at most one edge out of $u$, and similarly at $v \in R$. The edges $u \to v$ carrying flow form a matching whose size is the flow value.

Now take a minimum cut $(S,T)$. The cut $(\{s\}, \text{rest})$ has capacity $|L|$, so the minimum cut has capacity at most $|L|$ and cannot contain a huge edge. So if $u \in L \cap S$ and $uv$ is an edge, then $v \in S$. The edges leaving $S$ are therefore $s \to u$ for $u \in L \cap T$ and $v \to t$ for $v \in R \cap S$, and the capacity is $|L \cap T| + |R \cap S|$. The set $(L \cap T) \cup (R \cap S)$ is a vertex cover: an edge $uv$ with $u \notin T$ has $u \in S$, hence $v \in R \cap S$. Hence
$$\text{min cover} \le c(S,T) = \text{max flow} \le \text{max matching}.$$

blocks.title: Regular bipartite graphs have perfect matchings
blocks.body: Let $G$ be a bipartite graph with parts $L$, $R$ in which every vertex has degree $k \ge 1$. Prove that $G$ has a perfect matching.
blocks.solution:
Counting edges from each side gives $k|L| = k|R|$, so $|L| = |R|$. Use the network of the previous example. Put flow $1$ on each edge $s \to u$ and $v \to t$, and flow $1/k$ on each graph edge. Every $u \in L$ receives 1 and sends out $k \cdot \frac1k = 1$; every $v \in R$ receives $k \cdot \frac1k = 1$ and sends 1. This is a flow of value $|L|$.

So the maximum flow value is at least $|L|$, and it is at most $|L|$ by the cut $(\{s\}, \text{rest})$. By the integrality theorem there is an integer flow of value $|L|$, which is a matching covering all of $L$, and hence (as $|L| = |R|$) a perfect matching. The fractional flow was only a witness; integrality did the real work.

blocks.body:
- Cut capacity counts only edges from $S$ to $T$. Edges pointing back from $T$ into $S$ add nothing.
- Without backward residual edges, repeatedly pushing along paths can get stuck below the maximum, as in the five-edge example above.
- A minimum cut need not be unique, and neither need a maximum flow; the theorem only says their values agree.
- The integrality theorem says some maximum flow is integral, not every one: with edges $s \to a$, $s \to b$, $a \to c$, $b \to c$, $c \to t$ all of capacity 1, sending $\frac12$ along each of the routes through $a$ and through $b$ is also a maximum flow.

Max-flow min-cut is linear programming duality for one particular pair of programs; see [[linear-programming]] and [[convex-optimisation]]. Through the integrality theorem it proves Hall's theorem and König's theorem from [[cycles-matchings]], and Menger's theorem on disjoint paths. Minimum-cost flows, which add a price per unit on each edge, combine these ideas with the shortest-path algorithms of [[graph-algorithms]], and the running-time questions belong to [[algorithms]].

1. In the first worked example, raise the capacity of $a \to c$ from 6 to 8. What is the new maximum flow value? Give a minimum cut.
2. Show that for any flow $f$ and any two cuts $(S,T)$ and $(S',T')$, the net flows across them are equal.
3. Use flows to prove Hall's theorem: a bipartite graph has a matching covering $L$ if and only if every $A \subseteq L$ has at least $|A|$ neighbours.
4. Model this as a flow problem: three factories with outputs 5, 7, 4 must supply two shops needing 6 and 9, along given routes with given capacities.
